newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Major money centers split on March FOMC.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Major money centers split on March FOMC.

text.p: A Reuters sampling of economists in the world's primary trading centers found experts are divided about whether or not the U.S. Federal Reserve will raise official interest rates next week.

Six of 15 experts surveyed in New York, London and Tokyo said the Fed would tighten credit at Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. Four of these economists predicted an additional hike at the Fed's subsequent meeting in May.
One economist in Tokyo put the odds of a March hike at fifty percent. Four respondents predicted an interest-rate hike at the May meeting, but no move in March.

Of the remaining experts, one said the Fed will tighten later in the year, one forecast the central bank will hold the federal funds target steady at 5.25 percent for the remainder of the year, and two predict a Fed easing by yearend.

"Although recent data confirm the economy is roaring ahead in the first quarter, the question for the Fed is whether there is significant justification from an inflationary point of view for a rate rise now," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Banque Paribas' London office.

Wattret said the results of the Fed's latest "Beige Book" report on the economy pointed to benign inflation pressures, even in the labor market. "The Fed is looking for an inflationary trigger. It depends how pre-emptive they want to be," he said.
Many experts said the economy in the United States is growing faster than expected and inflation risks are tilted to the upside.
"The Fed will have to tap on the brakes a little bit," said Jim O'Sullivan, senior vice president at J.P. Morgan Securities Inc, who is calling for an upward rate move in March.
In particular, a pre-emptive move by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan would mostly arise from pressures in the labor market, O'Sullivan said.

"The labor market continues to show no sign of slowing. Wages have picked up, but so far, most of it has been offset by benefits," O'Sullivan said, adding "the offset from benefits has run its course and the employment cost index (ECI) will go up in 1997."
For the year as a whole, O'Sullivan is looking for the ECI to increase to 3.6 percent from 2.9 percent in 1996. The ECI for first-quarter 1997 is slated for release on April 29.
In other wage data, the U.S. Labor Department earlier in the month reported that February average hourly earnings rose modestly to $12.09 from $12.06 in January.
Analysts said much debate will pervade next week's meeting, citing no deterioration in labor cost inflation but no real threat in rising consumer prices either.

"It's a close call, but I don't expect to see a rate hike on March 25," said Akihiro Nishida, senior economist at Nikko Research Center in Tokyo. "In the longer term, there is a possiblity that the Fed may guide the fed funds rate to 5.5 percent by July, but the economy is forecast to slow down by the end of the year," he said.

John Ryding, managing director and senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co in New York, said an economy with sustained growth at around 3.0 percent may prompt the Fed to "take a little bit of a sting out."

"A (rate) move is by no means assured, we are only forecasting most likely outcomes," said Ryding, who is calling for no move in March but a rate hike in May. "The only outcome we can rule out this year is a cut in interest rates," he said.
